name: Kelp / seaweed supplements
short: Case reports: hyperthyroidism in a woman with no thyroid disease, and potential arsenic toxicity from a kelp supplement. In a 4-week trial, kelp capsules raised TSH in healthy adults.
text: In a 4-week double-blind trial in 36 healthy adults with normal thyroid function, kelp capsules taken by mouth significantly raised TSH at both doses and, at the higher dose, lowered total triiodothyronine; values returned to baseline 2 weeks after stopping, except TSH in the high-dose group, which was significantly decreased, and the authors said longer studies are needed to find out whether long-term use causes clinically significant thyroid disease. A case report described a 70-year-old woman with no previous thyroid disease who developed transient hyperthyroidism 3 months after taking kelp-containing tablets, which resolved after the tablets were stopped and antithyroid treatment was given; the authors attributed the risk to the high iodine content. A second case report, of what the authors called potential arsenic toxicosis, described a 54-year-old woman with alopecia, memory loss, rash, fatigue, nausea and vomiting, a raised urine arsenic level and arsenic in her daily kelp supplement, whose symptoms resolved within weeks of stopping it; in the same report, 8 of 9 kelp samples from health food stores had arsenic above a US food tolerance level, and none carried information on possible contamination with arsenic or other heavy metals. On the other side, an 8-week randomised trial in 50 overweight Japanese adults found no rise in thyroid hormone levels with an iodine-reduced kelp powder, in a population the authors describe as having a relatively high iodine intake from seaweed. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
